en: He grew apart, different from beasts.
In the hollows of the river Lob,
When my ten great herds lay there,
When horses' tongues darkened with green grass,
When the spring pasture ripened,
As the people moved toward the mountains,
When pale dawn broke,
When light fell upon the earth,
When I rode up and looked,
Wishing my horses well,
Among the horses, swirling,
A whirlwind was playing.
When I looked at the horses,
They cried out as though enemies had raided,
And played wildly.
When I rode up and looked,
There was no dam who had given birth,
No sire who had begotten him.
‘A true spirit-creature,’ I said,
And found him myself.
When I found Kula,
I slaughtered seven foals.
From the udders of seven mares,
I let him alone suckle.
I covered him with costly patterned cloth,
Had him tended apart from other beasts.
Giving him the name Akkula,
I tended him with special care.
My people were desperately hungry;
I led him here to sell.
I stopped before you,
My champion, to sell to you.
Cast your eye upon him, gray-maned one!
The wondrous steed whose like cannot be found,
I presented to you as a gift.
Keep a close eye upon him.
He is a champion, a living soul;
If you ride Akkula with care,
The four corners of the round world,
If you travel four times around,
He is a horse who will endure.
Girding a sword without a sheath,
The four corners of the round world,
Traveling four times around,
He is a horse for a lord to ride.
His whole tail is an armful;
His hooves are exceptional steel.
His wondrous prowess is quite apart;
Know it truly, my son Manas!
In an age his like cannot be found;
Not even a glimpse of his like is met.
He was met from the unseen.
The ill-omened swift horse
Was found in a precious place.
He is a whirlwind, a wind of a horse.
Rightly destined for you,
This is the moment of your meeting.
His broad croup is an armful;
He is a horse to ride to war,
If you sweep over mountain tops,
He has the power never to wear out.
Sent across hills, he will not flag;
He has exceptional qualities.
My lion, for you yourself,
He is a fitting horse.
No ordinary tail and mane,
This dear Akkula
Is no ordinary wandering horse.
Ridden to combat, he will not falter;
This dear Akkula
Shows the bearing of a skilled one.
Ridden to battle, he will not grow saddle-sore;
He shows the bearing of a seasoned one.
No ordinary tail and mane,
No ordinarily born horse.
His valor is well known;
He will endure a march to Beijing.
A most renowned, distinguished one,
He has the prowess of a wondrous steed.
Truly, Manas, gray-maned warrior,
He is a fitting horse.
Girding a black cutting sword,
Riding around Kara-Too,
He is a horse to ride on patrol.
Taking a tasseled spear in hand,
Scouting roads by day and night,
He is a horse to ride through hardship.
Keeping watch and tending the people,
Seeing lands no mortal has seen,
Seeing peoples no ear has heard of,
He is a horse to dispel longing.
Collar of gold, sleeves of bronze,
Double mail with lark-eye rings,
With golden crescents, no shot piercing it,
I longed for a man to wear it.
The foal of a young mare,
The Duldul of ordinary horses,
Who will not falter when ridden into combat,
Akkula, left forlorn,
I longed for his master to ride him.
Yesterday, from the river Lob,
Beyond Barbar, where no man goes,
From the hollow where waters pour,
Wild-ass plain, reed-grass ravine,
From the desert of Kurudum,
Encountered from the unseen,
Akkula, left forlorn,
Upon a masterless, sunless steppe,
Was found in empty land.
When a swan flew, its ears,
When a wild ass walked, its hooves,
Burned in that land.
No living thing trod there;
No spirit-creature knew to flee there.
There was no grass to nibble,
No water for a single sip in that land.
No traveler went there;
Whoever came upon that place
Did not remain alive, but died.
Wild bulls and wild camels,
When they raised dust from every corner,
Those who saw were astonished.
If living souls traveled,
Within that very desert,
Such creatures were found.
In the springtime season,
When the patchy snow departed,
When life returned to the grass,
When mares were foaling,
As a gift into my hands,
This Akkula was found.
‘A champion will ride him at last,’ I said,
And had him tended tenderly.
I hung an amulet upon his neck.
‘Someone may act as an enemy,’ I said;
I had earth dug and hid him,
Had him tended in a deep ravine.
When he reached his fourth year,
I fastened a halter upon his head.
So he would not escape our hands,
To that halter itself,
I attached twelve lead ropes,
And covered him with costly patterned cloth,
When leading that dark form,
Twelve strongmen led him without a rider.
‘He will maim whoever he meets,’ we said,
Clearing and opening his path.
He had such ways;
My khan Manas, listen:
For a round-headed mortal,
He was no horse one would encounter.
I had an expert fit him out,
Had a seer judge him.
Last year four, this year five,
He was found for your good fortune.
Akkula from the open steppe,
My magnanimous one, a Buraq horse for you,
My champion, has come to you.
This swine Akkula
Has no master to tether and ride him.
If a master is found for Kula,
The wondrous steed has no sense at all.
Winged, swift Akkula
Has come to you, leopard.
My valiant one touched by Kydyr,
The precious wondrous steed Akkula
Was found at the fitting moment.
My Akkula whom I tended
Is a supernatural swift horse.
He is endowed with sacred power.
I may sacrifice myself to God:
He has a master to ride him.
To you yourself, my champion,
Meeting upon the open steppe,
It is my time to give him.
The wheat heaped up,
My great people are desperately hungry;
I longed for it and asked you.
Broad chest, low mane,
Akkula, a horse to ride to war,
To you yourself, my champion,
I stand presenting him as a gift.
Accept Akkula;
The wheat heaped up,
Grant it to us!”
Then Manas said:
“Akkula, surpassing other beasts,
If Karacha presents him, I accept!
Let me heed your words.
The white wheat glowing red,
For this wondrous steed Akkula,
Let me give it in exchange for the gift.
Majestically stepping Akkula,
Grant him to us.
As a gift for Akkula,
All the white wheat,
Take it, leaving not one grain!”
After the hero said this,
Karacha stood shouting,
Calling his great host.
There were ninety red dromedaries.
Making the red dromedaries kneel,
Upon ninety dromedaries, the wheat
They loaded to the brim.
What remained after the ninety dromedaries,
They took in double handfuls and handfuls,
And put into their saddlebags.
‘A double handful of wheat is worth a yearling,’ they said,
And stood amazed.
Khan Manas, taking Akkula,
Stood with his heart at ease.
Karacha, taking wheat,
Had become rich.
Then Karacha,
Having given Akkula to Manas,
Turned toward Mecca in prayer,
Saying ‘Amen!’ and spreading his hands.
“My foal Manas, if you do not die,
You will draw blood from those who challenge you.
Of those who grapple with you,
None will survive; their souls will depart.
You are my lord, my lion;
My little people,
You are the one to protect them.
Keep gathering your army for battle.
Take care, my Manas:
‘How are you faring?’—
When Karacha grows old,
Keep asking how I fare!
You are a hero, you are a lion;
If the small people lose their senses,
You are the one to protect them!
Keep scouting and watching the land;
My land is the river Lob:
Keep seeking news from there!
May all your world be in balance;
Your charging enemies,
May their line be slaughtered and diminished!
You are my lord, my lion;
My champion has now been found.
You are the strength I take as support.
(Your prowess is well known.)
I shall gather my army as support;
Of your safety and your valor,
I shall ask the caravans.”
Thus saying, Karacha
Took an unblemished white-gray mare, it is said,
And slaughtered it in sacrifice, it is said.
Loading ninety camels,
Karacha went one way;
Riding Akkula, towering high,
Your magnanimous one set out another way.
Toward a spur beyond sight,
Toward an overhanging promontory,
Toward the edge of the rugged mountain,
Toward the face of a jutting ridge,
